name: Rule of 72
seoDesc: Rule of 72: work out doubling time from the increase. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Rule of 72 calculator returns doubling time from the field on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Rule of 72 calculator work?
sections.html:
The Rule of 72 calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports doubling time in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the increase.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html: • A measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Rule of 72 calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Doubling time=the natural log of (2) ÷ the natural log of (increase + 1)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Increase = 10 %. The calculator returns Doubling time = 7.272541.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Doubling time = 7.272541 should be roughly the size you expected from Increase = 10 %.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Rule of 72 calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the increase — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Rule of 72 calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — increase for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Switch the units to the ones you normally use and confirm the numbers are unchanged apart from their label; if they are not, a chip was on the wrong setting.

faq.q: What does the Rule of 72 calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns doubling time, derived from the increase. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Rule of 72 calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the increase, which is 1 field in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter increase in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Increase opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Doubling time = 7.272541. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Rule of 72 calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
